new_statements.quote: van den Berg 2009, p. 23: "The Awing language is a tonal language and exhibits three phonetic tone levels: low, mid and high; and two contour tones: rising and falling." ... "High tones become phonetically lower (mid) following low or falling tones. ... we treat all phonetic mid tones as the result of automatic downstep from high tone." — Fominyam 2021, p. 160: "In intonation languages like English or German, focalization can be achieved, among other means via prosody; for example, by stressing the focalized word/constituent within the sentence. This is not the case in (most) tonal languages like Awing."; p. 310: "such stressing rules are not applicable in a tonal language like Awing."
new_statements.citation: van den Berg, Bianca. 2009. A Phonological Sketch of Awing. Yaoundé: SIL Cameroon, §5 Tone, p. 23; supplemented by Fominyam, Henry Zamchang. 2021. Aspects of Awing grammar and information structure. PhD dissertation, Universität Potsdam, pp. 160 and 310.
new_statements.locator: van den Berg 2009 §5 'Tone', p. 23 (also §5.1 Automatic Downstep p. 23); Fominyam 2021 §4.4.2 p. 160 and ch. 6 p. 310
new_statements.rule_in_words: No source states where word stress falls. Awing is described as a tone language with underlying H vs L (phonetic mid = downstepped H) plus rising and falling contours on roots; the dedicated phonological sketch (van den Berg 2009) and the orthography guide (Alomofor & Anderson 2005/2007) never mention stress or accent. The only mention of stress in any source is Fominyam's remark, in a syntax discussion, that prominence-by-stressing (pitch-accent focus marking of the English/German type) is not applicable in tonal Awing; this is a statement about sentence-level focus prosody, not about word-level stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None (no stress rule given). Tone facts noted: noun-class prefixes are almost always L (a few archaic H prefixes mə́-/kə́-); consecutive verbs take an H nasal prefix; verb roots show two underlying patterns (H+HL, L+HL floating); grammatical tone marks habitual aspect.
new_statements.domain_note: van den Berg's tone data are citation (isolation) forms of single-root nouns (728) and verbs (770); orthography guide writes tone as pronounced in isolation. Fominyam's remarks concern focus marking at sentence level, where Awing uses a truncation mechanism instead of stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the Awing of Awing village (Santa subdivision, Mezam division, NW Cameroon), i.e. the main Mbwe'wi variety; the Seguin & Mbongue 1994 survey concerns the Bamukumbit dialect area and has no phonology. No dialect-specific stress claims exist.

sources.locator: van den Berg 2009 §5 'Tone', p. 23 (also §5.1 Automatic Downstep p. 23); Fominyam 2021 §4.4.2 p. 160 and ch. 6 p. 310
sources.note: Entire sketch (consonants, vowels, syllable structure, tone) never mentions stress or accent; §5 p. 23 states Awing is a tonal language with three phonetic levels (L, M, H; M = automatic downstep of H) and two contours (rising, falling); only 'emphasis' hit is about the second C of consonant clusters being 'pronounced with less emphasis' (p. 19).

sources.citation: Fominyam, Henry Zamchang. 2021. Aspects of Awing grammar and information structure. Doctoral dissertation, Universität Potsdam. xi+391 pp. DOI 10.25932/publishup-51806
sources.note: §1.7 Phonology (pp. 15-17) gives segment charts and a five-tone chart taken from Alomofor et al. (2007); no word-stress statement. Two passing remarks in syntax chapters: p. 160 'focalization can be achieved... by stressing the focalized word/constituent within the sentence. This is not the case in (most) tonal languages like Awing'; p. 310 'such stressing rules are not applicable in a tonal language like Awing'. 'Stressed pronouns' (p. 38) = strong/emphatic pronoun forms, not phonetic stress.

sources.citation: Alomofor, Christian (comp.). 2007. Awing – English Dictionary and English – Awing Index. Yaoundé: CABTAL. 220 pp. (Appendix pp. 197-212: 'Awing Orthography Guide' by Alomofor, Anderson & Hedinger)
sources.note: Appendix orthography guide (consonants, vowels, vowel length, diphthongs, tone, word division, long/short word forms) has no stress or accent statement; §3 Tone p. 206: 'Awing has three pitch levels (high, mid and low) and a variety of pitch glides between various levels'; tone written as pronounced in isolation. Only 'stress' hits are lexical entries (netaŋa 'hardship, stress').

sources.citation: Alomofor, Christian & Stephen C. Anderson. 2005. Awing Orthography Guide, December 2005 Revision. Yaoundé: SIL Cameroon. 16 pp.
sources.note: Table of contents (Alphabet, Consonants, Vowels, Vowel Length, Tone, Word Division, Elision, Punctuation) has no stress/accent section; body text layer is font-shifted (garbled) in this PDF, but the same guide is reproduced readably as the appendix of the 2007 dictionary (above), which contains no stress statement.
